solution: given: work \(= \alpha \cdot \beta^{2} \cdot e^{- \frac{x^{2}}{\alpha \cdot k.T}}\) \(k =\) boltzmann constant \(T =\) temperature \(x =\) displacement we know that, \(\frac{x^{2}}{\alpha.k.T} =\) dimensionless \[\left\lbrack \frac{x^{2}}{\alpha \cdot k \cdot T} \right\rbrack = \left\lbrack M^{0}{\text{ }L}^{0}{\text{ }T}^{0} \right\rbrack\] \[\lbrack\alpha\rbrack = \left\lbrack \frac{L^{2}}{K \cdot T} \right\rbrack\] \[\Rightarrow \lbrack K\rbrack = \left\lbrack M^{1}{\text{ }L}^{2}{\text{ }T}^{- 2}{\text{ }K}^{- 1} \right\rbrack\] \[\lbrack T\rbrack = \lbrack K\rbrack\] \[\Rightarrow \lbrack\alpha\rbrack = \left\lbrack \frac{L^{2}}{M^{1}{\text{ }L}^{2}{\text{ }T}^{- 2}{\text{ }K}^{- 1} \times K} \right\rbrack \Rightarrow \lbrack\alpha\rbrack = \left\lbrack M^{- 1}{\text{ }T}^{2} \right\rbrack\] \[\Rightarrow \omega = \alpha \cdot \beta^{2}\] \[\Rightarrow \frac{\left\lbrack M^{1}{\text{ }L}^{1}{\text{ }T}^{- 2} \right\rbrack\left\lbrack L \right\rbrack}{\left\lbrack M^{- 1}{\text{ }T}^{2} \right\rbrack} = \left\lbrack \beta^{2} \right\rbrack = \left\lbrack M^{2}{\text{ }L}^{2}{\text{ }T}^{- 4} \right\rbrack\] \[\lbrack\beta\rbrack = \left\lbrack {MLT}^{- 2} \right\rbrack\]
note: work = force x length, so the factor is [L], not [L^-1] (that gave L^0 instead of the M L^2 T^-2 the working needs)

solution: The bulb radiates \(1.25\%\) of \(1000\ W\), that is \(12.5\ W\). Treating it as a point source, the intensity at \(2\ m\) is \[I = \frac{P}{4\pi r^{2}} = \frac{12.5}{4\pi \times 4} = 0.2487\ W/m^{2}.\] With \(I = \frac{1}{2}c\varepsilon_{0}E_{0}^{2}\), \[E_{0} = \sqrt{\frac{2I}{c\varepsilon_{0}}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 0.2487}{3 \times 10^{8} \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12}}} = \sqrt{187.3} = 13.69\ V/m = 136.9 \times 10^{-1}\ V/m.\] To the nearest integer, \(x = 137\).
note: printed 0.249 gives sqrt(187.6)=13.70; the working's 187.3 and 13.69 come from I = 0.2487

solution:
In Dumas' method the nitrogen is collected over water, so the measured pressure must first be corrected for aqueous tension:
\(p_{N_{2}} = 715 - 15 = 700\ mm\ Hg = \frac{700}{760}\ atm = 0.9211\ atm\).

Moles of \(N_{2}\):
\(n = \frac{pV}{RT} = \frac{0.9211 \times 0.050}{0.0821 \times 300} = \frac{0.04605}{24.63} = 1.870 \times 10^{-3}\ mol\).

Each \(N_{2}\) carries two nitrogen atoms, so
mass of N \(= 2 \times 1.870 \times 10^{-3} \times 14 = 0.05236\ g = 52.36\ mg\).

Percentage of nitrogen \(= \frac{52.36}{292} \times 100 = 17.9\%\), nearest integer 18.
note: Last-digit slip: 2 x 1.870e-3 x 14 = 0.05236 g (52.36 mg), not 0.05235; the percentage line carries the same 52.36. 17.9% and the key 18 stand.

solution: In Carius sulphur estimation all the sulphur of the compound ends up as \(BaSO_4\). Molar mass of \(BaSO_4 = 137 + 32 + 4 \times 16 = 233\ u\), of which 32 u is sulphur. Mass of S \(= 1.4439 \times \frac{32}{233} = 0.19830\ g\). Percentage \(= \frac{0.19830}{0.471} \times 100 = 42.1\%\). Nearest integer 42.
note: Last-digit slip: 1.4439 x 32/233 = 0.198304, so 0.19830 g (not 0.19831); 42.1% and the key 42 stand.

solution: The nitrogen is collected over water, so its partial pressure is the total pressure less the aqueous tension, \(P_{N_{2}}=900-15=885\ mmHg\). Using \(n=PV/RT\) with \(P=885/760\ atm\), \(V=0.150\ L\) and \(T=300\ K\) gives \(n=\dfrac{(885/760)\times 0.150}{0.0821\times 300}=7.09\times 10^{-3}\ mol\). The mass of nitrogen is \(7.09\times 10^{-3}\times 28=0.1985\ g\), and since the sample taken was \(1\ g\) the percentage of nitrogen is \(19.85\%\). To the nearest integer the answer is 20.
note: Printed arithmetic: 7.09e-3 x 28 = 0.1985 g (not 0.1986), so 19.85%; the key 20 stands.

Since this is 25% of the sample, \(X = \frac{0.06818}{0.25} = 0.2727\ g = 272.7 \times 10^{-3}\ g\).

Cross-check with hydrogen: mass of H \(= 0.12 \times \frac{2}{18} = 0.01333\ g\), and \(X = \frac{0.01333}{0.0489} = 0.2726\ g\) -- consistent.

In Carius sulphur estimation every sulphur atom of the organic compound is precipitated as \(BaSO_{4}\), whose molar mass is \(233\text{ }g\text{ }mol^{-1}\) and which contains \(32\text{ }g\) of sulphur per mole. Mass of sulphur in the precipitate \(= \dfrac{32}{233}\times1.44 = 0.1978\text{ }g\). Percentage of sulphur \(= \dfrac{32 \times1.44}{233 \times0.471}\times100 = \dfrac{46.08}{109.743}\times100 = 41.99\%\). To the nearest integer the answer is \(42\).

solution:
The nitrogen is collected over water, so the measured pressure must be corrected for the aqueous tension:

\(p(N_{2}) = 715 - 15 = 700\) mm Hg.

Reduce the wet-gas volume to STP:

\(V_{STP} = \dfrac{p_{1}V_{1}}{T_{1}} \times \dfrac{T_{2}}{p_{2}} = \dfrac{700 \times 70}{300} \times \dfrac{273}{760} = 58.67\) mL.

Mass of nitrogen \(= \dfrac{58.67}{22400} \times 28 = 0.0733\) g.

Percentage of nitrogen \(= \dfrac{0.0733}{0.50} \times 100 = 14.66\%\), which to the nearest integer is 15.
note: Printed arithmetic: 0.0733/0.50 x 100 = 14.66, not 14.67; the key 15 stands.

solution: 'Volume strength' is the volume of \(O_2\) at STP liberated by unit volume of the solution: \(2H_2O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O + O_2\). So 1 L of a '25 volume' solution gives 25 L of \(O_2\) at STP. From the equation, 22.4 L of \(O_2\) at STP comes from 2 mol \(= 68\ g\) of \(H_2O_2\). Mass of \(H_2O_2\) per litre \(= \frac{68}{22.4} \times 25 = 75.9 \approx 76\ g\). Hence 1 L of the marketed solution contains about 76 g of \(H_2O_2\), nearest to the 75 g of option (B). (Equivalently, strength in g/L = volume strength \(\times\ 3.03\).)
note: Rounding slip: 68/22.4 x 25 = 75.9, which rounds to 76 g, not 75; key B (75 g) is the nearest option, so it stands.

solution: For a face-centred cubic lattice \(Z = 4\), and density is related to molar mass by \(d = \frac{ZM}{N_{A}a^{3}}\), so \(M = \frac{d\,N_{A}\,a^{3}}{Z}\). With \(a = 4.0 \times 10^{-8}\ cm\), \(a^{3} = 64 \times 10^{-24}\ cm^{3}\). Substituting, \(M = \frac{9.03 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} \times 64 \times 10^{-24}}{4} = 86.98\ g\ mol^{-1}\). To the nearest integer the atomic mass is \(87\).
note: Last-digit slip: 9.03 x 6.02 x 64/4 x 0.1 = 86.977, so 86.98 (not 86.97); the key 87 stands.

solution:
Check each statement against the two half-reactions.
(A) is correct: multiplying the anode half-reaction by \(n_{2}\) and the cathode half-reaction by \(n_{1}\) cancels the electrons and gives the stated overall equation.
(B) is correct: the electrons released at the anode are exactly those consumed at the cathode.
(C) is correct: \(n\) in the Nernst equation is the number of electrons transferred.
(D) is INCORRECT: reversible electrical work is the PRODUCT of the charge moved and the potential difference, \(w_{elec} = -nFE\), not their ratio.
note: Sentence 0 is left over from another question (a Nernst plot with n = 1, 2, 3 that this stem does not have); replaced by a neutral lead-in. The rest (D is incorrect: work is the PRODUCT nFE, not a ratio) is right and matches the key.

solution: Acetylation of aniline gives acetanilide in a 1:1 mole ratio, \(C_{6}H_{5}NH_{2}\rightarrow C_{6}H_{5}NHCOCH_{3}\). Aniline has \(M = 93\ g\ mol^{-1}\), so \(6.55\ g\) is \(6.55/93 = 0.0704\) mol. Acetanilide has \(M = 135\ g\ mol^{-1}\), so the maximum yield is \(0.0704\times135 = 9.50\ g\). Expressed as required, this is \(95.0\times10^{-1}\ g\), i.e. 95.
note: 0.0704 x 135 = 9.504, so 9.50 g and 95.0e-1 g (not 9.51 and 95.1); the key 95 stands.

solution: Track the sequence from nitrobenzene. (1) \(Br_{2}/FeBr_{3}\): the nitro group is a meta director, giving 3-bromonitrobenzene (1 Br). (2) \(Sn/HCl\) followed by (3) neutralisation reduces \(-NO_{2}\) to \(-NH_{2}\), giving 3-bromoaniline. (4) \(Br_{2}/H_{2}O\): the strongly activating \(-NH_{2}\) group brominates every free position ortho and para to itself, i.e. C-2, C-4 and C-6, giving 2,3,4,6-tetrabromoaniline (4 Br). (5) \(NaNO_{2}/HBr\) at \(0-5^{\circ}C\) converts \(-NH_{2}\) into the diazonium salt, and (6) \(CuBr/NaBr\) (Sandmeyer) replaces \(-N_{2}^{+}\) by \(-Br\), adding a fifth bromine. Product (P) is pentabromobenzene (Br at 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6), i.e. the tetrabromo ring plus the new Br, a total of \(5\) bromine atoms.
note: The named product was wrong: Sandmeyer on 2,3,4,6-tetrabromoaniline replaces NH2 by Br, giving pentabromobenzene (Br at 1,2,3,4,6), 5 Br as the key says.

solution:
Successive ionisation enthalpies rise gradually while electrons come from the valence shell, then jump sharply once the valence shell is empty and the next electron must come from the noble-gas core.

Here \(IE_1 = 800\), \(IE_2 = 2427\), \(IE_3 = 3658\) and \(IE_4 = 25024\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\). The first three rise by factors of about 3 and 1.5, but \(IE_4\) is nearly seven times \(IE_3\). So the atom has exactly three valence electrons, and it belongs to group 13 (these are boron's values).

Group 2 would show the jump after \(IE_2\), group 14 after \(IE_4\). (The fifth value, 32824, is larger than the fourth, as each successive ionisation enthalpy must be; boron's fifth is about 32 830 \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\).)
note: The remark said the paper prints 2824; this stem prints 32824 (and boron's fifth is about 32 830), so the remark is reworded to match.

solution:
Converting \(\mathrm{Li(g) \rightarrow Li^{2+}(g) + 2e^{-}}\) needs the first plus the second ionisation enthalpy: \(520 + 7297 = 7817\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\).

Moles of lithium: \(n = \frac{3.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{g}}{7\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 5\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol}\).

Energy required: \(7817\times5\times10^{-4} = 3.91\ \mathrm{kJ}\), which is 4 to the nearest integer. (The quantity asked for is the energy for 3.5 mg, in kJ, not per mole.)
note: The remark said the paper prints kJ per mole; this stem prints kJ, so the remark now just states what is asked.
